walkthroughs.body_html:
Three forms, same equation:

F = m × a
a = F ÷ m
m = F ÷ a

Always use the resultant force in F = ma — not just one of the forces.

Weight is a force, so it can be the resultant force too.

A 2 kg ball in free fall: weight = 2 × 10 = 20 N. Resultant force = 20 N. Acceleration = 20 ÷ 2 = 10 m/s². ✅

That's why everything falls at the same rate (ignoring air resistance).

Inertial mass = F ÷ a. It measures how stubborn an object is when you try to accelerate it.

Apply 50 N to a trolley and it accelerates at 5 m/s². Its inertial mass is 50 ÷ 5 = 10 kg.

For GCSE, inertial mass equals normal (gravitational) mass — phew.

mcqs.q: Rearranging F = ma to find mass gives:
A constant resultant force on an object causes:
If an object is moving at constant velocity in a straight line, what is the net force on it?
options: Only when the force is small enough to be ignored.
There must be a forward force on the object to keep it moving.
Zero — by Newton's first law, constant velocity requires zero net force.
The net force equals the velocity times the mass of the object.

mcqs.q: If a car has negative acceleration, what does that necessarily mean?
options: The net force equals the velocity times the mass of the object.
Negative acceleration always means the car is slowing down.
Negative acceleration means the car is moving backwards.
Its acceleration is in the negative direction (often opposite to the chosen positive direction); it may be slowing down or speeding up in reverse.

mcqs.q: Does Hooke's law apply to a spring for any amount of stretching?
options: Negative acceleration means the car is moving backwards.
Yes — Hooke's law applies to any spring at any extension.
No — it only holds up to the limit of proportionality; beyond that the relationship between force and extension is no longer linear.
Only when the force is small enough to be ignored.
